title: Plans
goal: Talk about the future in a language with no future tense, and soften every request with one inserted syllable you've been using since unit 6 without realizing it.
bekal: express plans with the present tense, *aion* and *ajattelin*
use the **-isi-** insert for politeness and hypotheticals
finish A1 knowing exactly what your next step is

dialogs.title: Dialog — Mitä seuraavaksi?
dialogs.intro: The last evening before Aino moves to Tampere for a new job. The three of them at the same café.

notes: **Finnish has no future tense at all.** *Valmistun keväällä* uses the present tense and means "I'll graduate in the spring". The time expression carries the future, not the verb — just as in English "I'm leaving tomorrow". It's a saving people rarely mention when they warn you how hard Finnish is.

**Voisitko, tekisin, tulisin, olisin** — all use the **-isi-** insert. It marks something hypothetical, and that's exactly why it works as a politeness tool: asking hypothetically sounds softer than asking directly, just like English "could you" and "would you". The *saisinko* you've used since unit 6 is this same form.

**Jos löytäisin** — in a hypothetical sentence, **both halves** take *-isi-*: *Tekisin nasi gorengia, jos löytäisin mausteet.* English marks it with "would" in one half and a past form in the other; Finnish uses the same marker twice.

**Ajattelin tulla** — the past tense of *ajatella*, but it means a future plan: "I was thinking of coming". It sounds lighter and less binding than *aion tulla* (I intend to come), and Finns use it all the time for tentative suggestions — just like the English phrase.
**Kahden tunnin päässä** — "at a distance of two hours". Distance is expressed in time, just as in English: "two hours away".
**Tulette käymään** — after a verb of motion, the *-maan/-mään* ending. The pattern from unit 12, and here it sounds like an invitation, not an order.

grammars.title: The future without a future tense
body: Three ways to state plans, from the most neutral to the most binding. None of them uses a special verb form.
after: **The time expression decides the time.** *Menen kauppaan* can mean "I'm going to the shop" or "I'll go to the shop"; *huomenna menen kauppaan* can't be misunderstood.
If you really want to stress that something hasn't happened yet, use *aion* or add the time. Otherwise, the present tense is enough and actually sounds the most natural.
⚠️ Don't look for an equivalent of *will* or *going to*. There isn't one, and searching for it only makes your sentences go round in circles.

grammars.title: The -isi- insert for politeness and hypotheticals
body: One insert, two equally important uses: softening requests, and expressing "what if". The form is exactly the same for both.
after: **For politeness** — compare the steps: *Anna se.* (give it) → *Voitko antaa sen?* (can you give it?) → *Voisitko antaa sen?* (could you give it?). The last is the softest, and the one used most with people you don't know well.
**Most useful to learn right now**: *saisinko* (could I have), *voisitko* (could you), *haluaisin* (I'd like), *olisiko* (would there be). These four cover almost every polite everyday request.
**For hypotheticals** — *jos* in one half, *-isi-* in both halves: *Jos minulla olisi aikaa, menisin Lappiin.* (If I had time, I'd go to Lapland.)

blocks.text: The last line is the sentence that will change your experience of Finland the most — and it's the one you learned in unit 1, now in a softer form. The circle closes.

These twenty units cover all of A1 and touch on a few points of A2. If you've really done the exercises, you can now do the following — and this list isn't a publisher's promise, but a summary of the material you've worked through.

items: Introduce yourself: where you're from, where you live, your age, family and job.
Use the six place endings and know when to use the "inside" and "outside" groups.
Build present, past and perfect sentences, positive and negative.
Tell a whole object from a partial one — the most typically Finnish distinction of all.
Shop, order, make appointments, ask for directions and describe symptoms.
Read rental ads, fill in simple forms and get through a short interview.
Make polite sentences with *-isi-* — and know why they sound polite.

blocks.title: Four steps that really move the needle
items: **Speak every day, even just three sentences.** Skills you don't use shrink faster than you'd think. Three sentences a day beat three hours once a week.
**Write three sentences about your day every evening** — one positive, one negative, one question. The habit from unit 14, and still the one that pays off most.
**Watch with Finnish subtitles, not English ones.** Yle Areena is free and full of Finnish shows with subtitles. It's hard at first; after two months it feels like a free class every day.
**Don't let people switch to English.** This matters most and is ignored most often. One sentence — *Voisimmeko puhua suomea? Minä opiskelen.* — saves hours of lost practice.

blocks.text: The next official step is **A2**: longer compound sentences, plurals with full endings, the *-va/-nut* forms as adjectives, and subjectless verbs you can form yourself from any verb. All of it stands on what you've mastered here; none of it starts from zero again.
